extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, policymakers, and thinkers concerned with limits of government and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance on when and how government should intervene in social affairs (especially education, marriage, and administration), balancing individual liberty, local autonomy, and centralized information/oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: State education only as one among many experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: The State should only exist, if it exist at all, as one among many competing experiments, carried on for the purpose of example and stimulus; the government may undertake schools and universities only when society could not or would not provide proper institutions of education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the voluntary principle where possible; if sufficient private persons are available to provide education under government auspices, they could give equally good education voluntarily. Government provision is justifiable chiefly when private provision is absent or impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory education enforced by public examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The instrument for enforcing the law could be no other than public examinations, extending to all children, and beginning at an early age. An age might be fixed at which every child must be examined to ascertain if he (or she) is able to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a child proves unable, the father, unless he has sufficient ground of excuse, might be subjected to a moderate fine (to be worked out by his labour), and the child might be sent to school at his expense. Examinations should be renewed annually with a gradually extending range of subjects to make the universal acquisition and retention of a certain minimum of general knowledge virtually compulsory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary advanced examinations and non-privileging of certificates
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond the minimum, there should be voluntary examinations on all subjects, at which all who come up to a certain standard of proficiency might claim a certificate. Degrees or public certificates of scientific or professional acquirements should be given to all who present themselves for examination and stand the test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such certificates should confer no advantage over competitors other than the weight attached by public opinion; governments should not be allowed to exclude anyone from professions on alleged deficiency of qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit examination content to facts and positive science; avoid testing opinions' truth
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent the State from exercising an improper influence over opinion, the knowledge required for passing an examination (beyond instrumental parts such as languages) should be confined to facts and positive science exclusively. Examinations on religion, politics, or other disputed topics should not turn on the truth or falsehood of opinions, but on the matter of fact that such and such an opinion is held, on such grounds, by such authors, schools, or churches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach allows citizens to be instructed about disputed subjects without the State biasing the conclusions; a student may be examined in the arguments or history of doctrines without being required to profess belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-branch examinations must be voluntary; avoid governmental gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: The examinations in the higher branches of knowledge should be entirely voluntary. It would be too dangerous a power to governments were they allowed to exclude any one from professions, even from the profession of teacher, for alleged deficiency of qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain voluntary participation and prevent official exclusion from careers based on state-controlled credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental responsibility and permissible marital regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact of causing the existence of a human being is one of the most responsible actions. To undertake this responsibility unless the being will have at least ordinary chances of a desirable existence is a crime against that being. In a country over-peopled, to produce children beyond a very small number, with the effect of reducing the reward of labour, is a serious offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws that forbid marriage unless parties can show means of support do not exceed legitimate powers of the State; whether such laws are expedient depends on local circumstances and feelings, but they are not objectionable as violations of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer individual provision when individuals can do the thing better
rubrics_metrics.description: When the thing to be done is likely to be better done by individuals than by the government — speaking generally, there is no one so fit to conduct any business as those who are personally interested in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle condemns legislative and governmental interferences with ordinary processes of industry and endorses leaving many functions to those with personal stakes in outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave certain tasks to individuals to cultivate civic faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cases, though individuals may not do the particular thing so well on average as officers of government, it is desirable that it should be done by them rather than by the government as a means to their own mental education—strengthening active faculties, exercising judgment, and giving familiar knowledge of subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recommends jury trial, free local and municipal institutions, and voluntary associations as vital to the political education of citizens; such habits and powers are necessary for the working and preservation of a free constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of functions in government to prevent patronage and bureaucracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every function superadded to those already exercised by the government causes its influence over hopes and fears to be more widely diffused, and converts the active and ambitious part of the public into hangers-on of the government, or of some party which aims at becoming the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If major enterprises (roads, railways, banks, universities, charities) were branches of government with employees appointed and paid by it, neither freedom of the press nor representative legislature could secure real freedom; concentration of functions creates clientelism and entrenched bureaucracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralize information; disseminate power — test for arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical principle in which safety resides: the greatest dissemination of power consistent with efficiency; but the greatest possible centralization of information, and diffusion of it from the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize municipal administration with minute division of local officers for local matters while maintaining a central superintendence to concentrate experience, know all that is done, and make knowledge acquired in one place available to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central superintendence: right to know and limited coercive power
rubrics_metrics.description: The central organ should concentrate the variety of information and experience derived from conduct of public business in all localities; it should have a right to know all that is done and a special duty to make the knowledge acquired in one place available for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its actual power should be limited to compelling local officers to obey laws laid down for guidance; in matters not provided for by general rules, local officers should be left to their judgment and held responsible to their constituents; violations should be addressed by tribunals or constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative coercion justified only for national interest or to cure widespread harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers of administrative coercion and subordinate legislation are justifiable in cases of first-rate national interest or for the cure of rooted habits of maladministration in matters affecting the whole community, but would be out of place in the superintendence of interests purely local.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use central coercive powers sparingly and only when local mismanagement overflows into other localities or impairs the moral and physical condition of the whole labouring community (Poor Law Board example).

rubrics_metrics.name: State's useful role is depository and diffuser of experience, not substitute actor
rubrics_metrics.description: What the State can usefully do is to make itself a central depository, and active circulator and diffuser, of the experience resulting from many trials; its business is to enable each experimentalist to benefit by the experiments of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government should inform, advise, and, on occasion, denounce — aiding and stimulating individual exertion — but mischief begins when it substitutes its own activity for that of individuals or bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of concentrating talent in bureaucracy via civil-service selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting all members of the civil service by competitive examination to obtain the most intelligent persons has been proposed; opponents argue that permanent official service does not hold out sufficient prospects to attract the highest talents, but if all high talent were drawn into government service it might concentrate culture and intelligence in a bureaucracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: drawing the nation's leading talent into government risks concentrating ability, creating a bureaucracy that others look to for direction and potentially making reforms contrary to the bureau's interest impossible.
